extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv instructors, and performers of comedy/theatre improvisation
extracted.subtask_description: Practical handbook-style guidelines and evaluative principles for learning, teaching, directing, and performing comedic improvisation across formats (short form, long form, competitive, theatrical, and televised).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: The authentic, in-the-moment creation of material rather than premeditated lines; improvisation’s defining quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors emphasize presence and freshness as central to improv’s power; spontaneity can liberate and inspire but is also a skill that workshops and exercises aim to cultivate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saying Yes (Accepting Offers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept offers from scene partners rather than blocking or negating them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a core technique to keep scenes moving and collaborative; linked to exercises and games that practice acceptance and development of offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: What Comes Next (Forward Momentum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always advance the scene by answering the implicit question 'what happens next' rather than stalling or merely reacting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter-level principle for generating story or action; includes exercises and examples showing how to push scenes forward while maintaining truth and surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status (High/Low Status Dynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of status relationships between characters to create shape, comedy, and scene dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Status ladder, status switches and status triggers are taught as tools; authors give examples, exercises and warnings about balancing status play so it serves story and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding the Game in the Scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Detecting and exploiting a repeating pattern, premise, or conceit (the 'game') that can be heightened for comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book teaches identifying the game as vital to scene architecture; includes methods for discovering, committing to, and amplifying the game while avoiding trivial or obvious repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working Together / Collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritising ensemble support, joining, and mutual listening over individual showboating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice and exercises focus on joining partners, sharing offers, avoiding competitiveness that harms the scene, and building ensemble identity and style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being Changed (Reacting / Letting the Scene Affect You)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing characters and performers to be transformed by the scene rather than remaining static.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages genuine reacting and emotional truth to create stakes and depth; presented as complementing comic invention and story arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playing Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating distinct, truthful characters with clear objectives, names, and relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers choices for characterisation, when to exaggerate or ground a character, and techniques for sustaining distinct roles across scenes or long-form shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing Format (Short Form vs Long Form vs Games vs Scenes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the performance format that best suits the troupe’s talents and the goals of the show (games, montage, Harold, narrative, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors argue to 'pick the format which will exploit your talents' and to ask 'Would this be better if it were scripted?'; explain trade-offs: games bring audience interaction and hooks; long form allows threads and deeper story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Suggestions: Use and Abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: How and when to use audience suggestions—valuable as a spur for spontaneity but easy to overuse or abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns of the 'skateboarding duck' effect where audiences admire the process instead of the story; suggests sparing, purposeful use and techniques (e.g., refueling Harold) to incorporate suggestions without distracting from content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk and Failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Encouraging risk-taking and accepting failure as central to exciting improv.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors stress that risk makes improv thrilling; recommend building mechanisms into shows to allow and celebrate failures (forfeits, visible scoring, audience reaction) so performers feel safe to take risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance Process vs Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid letting the fact of improvisation (the process) become the primary spectacle at the expense of story, character, or craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While process is important and not 'evil', the book repeatedly warns against format choices that foreground novelty and process over quality of performance and audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition and Its Effects (Theatresports / Improv Tournaments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines for staging competitive improv: how competition energizes but can also corrupt spirit and quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice includes using 'scratch' teams to avoid unhealthy fixed-team competitiveness, judges' flexibility to prioritize entertainment over fairness, and being cautious about national-pride dynamics in tournaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring & Elimination Formats (Micetro/Maestro)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of audience scoring and elimination formats to manage large casts and to maintain quality over a show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Micetro is praised for keeping standards high and creating a climactic arc but warned to be frank about scoring unfairness (all players in a scene get same score) and the emotional sting of elimination; works best with mixed ability groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directing on Stage / Gorilla Theatre
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics and evaluation of having performers direct each other publicly and audience-judged directing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public directing can keep quality high; directors should boldly announce intentions to give audience a yardstick; mechanisms exist for penalising unsuccessful directors to keep the show entertaining and risk-friendly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harold and Long-form Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-form approach presenting multiple strands that may connect, emphasizing editing, callbacks, and structural connections over single continuous narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes variations (tight three-part Harold vs open exploration), the Armando/monologue variation, and practical options like 'refueling' with multiple suggestions; warns that long-form can be either more or less unified than short-form depending on choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improv for TV vs Live Performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles for using improvisation in recorded media: TV reduces perceived risk and requires different handling than live performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On-camera improv often becomes a behind-the-scenes writing tool or is edited for best moments (e.g., Christopher Guest films). Live improv’s risk is part of the attraction; TV may use improvisation to achieve naturalistic acting but impacts audience perception of risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms to Incorporate Failure into the Show
rubrics_metrics.description: Design show elements that convert mistakes into entertainment so performers can take risks safely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include fake or playful scoring, forfeits, public forfeit rituals, and MC/judge behaviors that frame failure as part of the fun rather than shameful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling and Narrative Drive
rubrics_metrics.description: Using story elements (forward-seeking narrative, stakes, connected subplots) to create investment and repeat audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note that shows with ongoing storylines (e.g., soap-style improv) create audience return; narrative gives purpose beyond cleverness and can coexist with improv’s spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Reference vs Maintaining the Fourth Wall
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the show will acknowledge its format/audience/process or maintain theatrical illusion throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows can be anywhere on this axis; games and short-form tend to be self-referential with audience hooks, while some Harolds or narrative pieces keep the fourth wall intact. Choice affects tone and audience expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and Scene Transitions (In-Performance Direction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill in ending scenes, cutting to new ones, and editing live to maintain rhythm and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvisers should learn to 'edit' each other—ending scenes, starting new ones from nothing—to shape the performance; directors and MCs are tools for managing pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using Improvisation as a Rehearsal/Writing Tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisation’s role in generating material for scripted work: a development process distinct from public improvisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spolin/Boal tradition views improv primarily as rehearsal; the book documents both uses—development vs performance—and explains when each is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting and Shaping Audience Interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentional use of volunteers and suggestions only when they advance the show or suit the format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors caution against gratuitous audience involvement; interaction should serve the story or the show’s design rather than being novelty for novelty’s sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching and Workshop Design
rubrics_metrics.description: Structuring classes and exercises to keep actors 'in the present', build spontaneity, and develop ensemble skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book models Section Two on their workshops: warm-ups, games, and sequenced exercises are recommended; teachers should be aware of risks of certain exercises and adapt to student levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick the Medium that Exploits Your Talents
rubrics_metrics.description: Constantly evaluate whether the chosen improvisational medium (live, TV, narrative, game-based) best showcases the performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors repeatedly advise asking 'Would this be better if it were scripted?' and choosing formats (e.g., TellTales, DreamDate) that play to the company’s strengths rather than forcing a fashionable form.
